article_title: Zooming in: The role of nonverbal behavior in sensing the quality of collaborative group engagement
citation: Paneth, L., Jeitziner, L. T., Rack, O., Opwis, K., & Zahn, C. (2024). Zooming in: The role of nonverbal behavior in sensing the quality of collaborative group engagement. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09422-7
title: Quality of Collaborative Group Engagement (QCGE): a shared, multifaceted, dynamic, contextualized four-dimension group-process construct for CSCL
description: The paper builds on Sinha et al. (2015)'s conceptualization of the quality of collaborative group engagement, which groups 'the quality of collaborative group engagement (QCGE) as shared, multifaceted, dynamic, and contextualized'. Four dimensions are distinguished: behavioral engagement (on-task persistence and effort), social engagement (quality of socio-emotional group interactions), cognitive engagement (collaborative development of understanding via monitoring, planning, evaluating), and conceptual-to-consequential engagement (solving meaningful problems with disciplinary practices and content as conceptual tools). The study treats engagement as fluctuating phases, not a fixed state.
requirements: Requires a QCGE rating scheme applied to video segments of group collaboration, rated low/moderate/high per dimension
constraints: Conceptualizations comprehensive for CSCL contexts emerged only recently and definitions of student engagement lack standard descriptions, per the article
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving
regulation of group learning
domain-specific knowledge building
examples: The study applied the rating scheme to 1-min video segments of 38 triads collaborating on a Sweet Home 3D office design task
key_sources: Paneth, L., Jeitziner, L. T., Rack, O., Opwis, K., & Zahn, C. (2024). Zooming in: The role of nonverbal behavior in sensing the quality of collaborative group engagement. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09422-7

article_title: Measuring the quality of collaborative group engagement: Development and validation of the QCGE self-assessment scale (QCGE-SAS)
citation: Loris T. Jeitziner, Lisa Paneth, Oliver Rack, Susanne Bleisch, Carmen Zahn. (2025). Measuring the quality of collaborative group engagement: Development and validation of the QCGE self-assessment scale (QCGE-SAS). Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09445-8
title: QCGE-SAS: a standardised self-assessment scale for quality of collaborative group engagement in higher education CSCL
description: The QCGE-SAS is a pragmatic group-level self-assessment instrument operationalising QCGE across behavioural, social, cognitive, and conceptual-to-consequential dimensions with items phrased in first-person plural (e.g. asking about "the subjective experience of the group's collaborative participation during the task"). Items were derived from Sinha et al.'s (2015) QCGE rating scheme, reviewed by an expert panel, and rated on a seven-point Likert scale from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'. The article positions it as complementing resource-intensive observation-based procedures and multi-method measurement.
requirements: Items take the group as the unit of analysis, worded to make individuals identify with the group as a unit rather than as individuals, and respondents answer about their learning group's collaborative task
constraints: Validated for higher education contexts (undergraduate and postgraduate students in one School of Applied Psychology); the social engagement subscale showed unacceptable reliability
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: quality of collaborative group engagement in CSCL tasks
examples: Administered at the end of courses and at the end of a laboratory CSCL study with groups of three; items were presented in randomised order
key_sources: Loris T. Jeitziner, Lisa Paneth, Oliver Rack, Susanne Bleisch, Carmen Zahn. (2025). Measuring the quality of collaborative group engagement: Development and validation of the QCGE self-assessment scale (QCGE-SAS). Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09445-8

article_title: Measuring the quality of collaborative group engagement: Development and validation of the QCGE self-assessment scale (QCGE-SAS)
citation: Loris T. Jeitziner, Lisa Paneth, Oliver Rack, Susanne Bleisch, Carmen Zahn. (2025). Measuring the quality of collaborative group engagement: Development and validation of the QCGE self-assessment scale (QCGE-SAS). Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09445-8
title: QCGE framework: four dimensions of quality of collaborative group engagement at group level
description: The QCGE construct, from Sinha et al. (2015) and elaborated by Rogat et al. (2022), conceptualises engagement as shared, contextualised and multidimensional at the group level: "behavioural engagement (BE) includes persistence and effort in the task; social engagement (SE) involves the quality of group interactions"; cognitive engagement covers task-centred planning, structuring and monitoring; and conceptual-to-consequential engagement covers using domain-specific methods and connecting ideas to prior knowledge. The article treats QCGE as a key element of shared regulation of learning in CSCL and builds its scale directly on this framework.
requirements: Observable indicators per dimension (on-/off-task behaviour, balanced participation, planning and monitoring, evidence use) ground the rating scheme that the self-assessment items derive from
constraints: Conceptualised for collaborative learning in complex digital learning environments; the dimensions are interrelated rather than independent, and low-quality behavioural sequences can even support cohesion
target_learners: student learning groups in higher education
target_learning_goals: dimension-specific and overall quality of collaborative group engagement
examples: Sinha et al. (2015) tested the framework with ten groups using an observational approach; this article operationalised it as a self-assessment scale for higher education

article_title: A Hands-On Quantum Cryptography Workshop For Pre-University Students
citation: Adrian Nugraha Utama, Jianwei Lee, and Mathias Alexander Seidler. (2020). A Hands-On Quantum Cryptography Workshop For Pre-University Students. arXiv:1911.02565v2 [physics.ed-ph]. https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02565v2
title: Released Arduino and Python control programs with full documentation on GitHub
description: The workshop's experimental sequence is automated with Arduino microcontrollers and Python programs that synchronize the quantum and classical channels and generate each bit consistently. The article states: "The sequence was executed using Arduino and Python programs. These are fully documented and available on Github." The release is intended to facilitate educators in conducting the workshop, and the authors believe the simplified implementation "is an easily deployable and engaging QKD demonstration that can be realized by a wide range of educational institutions."
requirements: Arduino microcontrollers for laser and motor control and photodiode readout, plus Python programs for protocol automation
constraints: The overall duration required to generate each "qubit" (1.5 s) is limited by the stepper motors' maximum rotation speed of about 10 rpm
target_learning_goals: operating a BB84 key distribution experiment
assembling and operating experimental apparatus for encrypted message distribution
examples: The codes and technical documentation are available at the GitHub repository cited in the article's footnote 24
key_sources: Adrian Nugraha Utama, Jianwei Lee, and Mathias Alexander Seidler. (2020). A Hands-On Quantum Cryptography Workshop For Pre-University Students. arXiv:1911.02565v2 [physics.ed-ph]. https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02565

article_title: Teaching Quantum Computing to High School Students
citation: Ciaran Hughes, Joshua Isaacson, Anastasia Perry, Ranbel Sun, and Jessica Turner. (2020). Teaching Quantum Computing to High School Students. https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.07206
title: Three labeled difficulty levels with skippable sections let one module serve diverse student backgrounds
description: The course was "designed with three diﬀerent levels of complexity depending on the students’ experience with mathematics and abstract reasoning". All sections and problems are labeled by difficulty level, and intermediate and advanced sections within each chapter are labeled so students and teachers can skip them. Chapters can be skipped while leaving the core content fully understandable, and Fig. 1 outlines minimum recommended prerequisites for each unit for those with limited time.
requirements: Teachers should use knowledge of students' strengths to guide their choice of topics, as outlined in Fig. 1
constraints: Given usual constraints on teaching time, the materials are suggested for use after AP examinations, in an extracurricular club, or as an independent project resource
target_learners: high school students with diverse mathematics and physics backgrounds
target_learning_goals: quantum computing concepts at levels matched to students' mathematical and abstract-reasoning experience
examples: Students with strong mathematics and computer science backgrounds but rudimentary physics knowledge engaged well with mathematical and programming activities but struggled with Stern-Gerlach apparatus, beam splitters, and phase shifts, so more focus was given to the mathematical formulation
key_sources: Ciaran Hughes, Joshua Isaacson, Anastasia Perry, Ranbel Sun, and Jessica Turner. (2020). Teaching Quantum Computing to High School Students. https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.07206

article_title: A Framework for Curriculum Transformation in Quantum Information Science and Technology Education
citation: Simon Goorney, Jonas Bley, Stefan Heusler, Jacob Sherson. (2024). A Framework for Curriculum Transformation in Quantum Information Science and Technology Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10371
title: The Quantum Curriculum Transformation Framework (QCTF): a four-step decision-tree for QIST curriculum design
description: The QCTF is a decision-tree based methodology for designing and transforming QIST educational material, structured as a what-why-how sequence akin to backwards design. It moves from content selection via the European Competence Framework, through targeted skills and Bloom-based learning goals, to teaching approaches grounded in didactical research. As the authors state, "The Quantum Curriculum Transformation Framework (QCTF) consists of four steps: 1. choose a topic, 2. choose one or more targeted skills, 3. choose a learning goal and 4. choose a teaching approach that achieves this goal." Subsections may be used independently, and the framework is intended to be extended as new research results emerge.
requirements: Practitioners follow the decision tree from topic selection through to a teaching approach matched to the chosen learning goal
constraints: The framework is presented as intended for future testing and refinement, not yet empirically validated; subsections may be used when the complete framework is not applicable
target_learners: University Bachelor and Master students in STEM fields entering the quantum workforce
target_learning_goals: Clearly defined educational goals and outcomes in QIST courses and programs
examples: An example curriculum on quantum communication basics and an example lesson on quantum teleportation are worked through the framework's steps
key_sources: Simon Goorney, Jonas Bley, Stefan Heusler, Jacob Sherson. (2024). A Framework for Curriculum Transformation in Quantum Information Science and Technology Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10371

article_title: Quantum Computing, Math, and Physics (QCaMP): Introducing quantum computing in high schools
citation: Megan Ivory, Alisa Bettale, Rachel Boren, Ashlyn D. Burch, Jake Douglass, Lisa Hackett, Boris Kiefer, Alina Kononov, Maryanne Long, Mekena Metcalf, Tzula B. Propp, Mohan Sarovar. (2023). Quantum Computing, Math, and Physics (QCaMP): Introducing quantum computing in high schools. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16788
title: QCaMP curriculum: a week-long, no-prerequisites sequence from classical bits to an IBM Q research project
description: QCaMP's 2022 curriculum is a five-day module sequence — classical bits and gates, probability and statistics, light labs covering double slit and polarization, superposition and the Hadamard gate, entanglement, and an IBM Q research project with virtual lab tours — developed collaboratively by QIST researchers from national laboratories and academia. Its aim was to make material accessible "by avoiding any prerequisite math, physics, or computer science courses and to incorporate experiential and active learning wherever possible." Each day ended with an anonymous Padlet Q&A whose misconceptions were addressed the next morning. Teacher and student curricula were largely the same, with teacher camps adding pedagogical discussion and student camps adding career talks. A shipped materials kit supporting the hands-on modules cost $138.20 per participant.
requirements: Delivery required shipping hands-on materials (lasers, apertures, polarizers, dice, Q is for Quantum) to participants before the virtual camp began
constraints: The CHSH activity developed for entanglement was found too advanced for the audience and was significantly modified for the student camp to a conceptual discussion of entanglement versus classical correlation
target_learners: High school students and middle/high school teachers with no assumed background knowledge in quantum topics
target_learning_goals: Foundational quantum information science concepts including bits, gates, superposition, measurement, and entanglement; probability and statistics for interpreting quantum experiment outcomes
examples: The 2022 camps taught 32 students and 20 teachers over two one-week virtual camps, with each day ending in a Padlet Q&A session used to address misconceptions the following morning
key_sources: Megan Ivory, Alisa Bettale, Rachel Boren, Ashlyn D. Burch, Jake Douglass, Lisa Hackett, Boris Kiefer, Alina Kononov, Maryanne Long, Mekena Metcalf, Tzula B. Propp, Mohan Sarovar. (2023). Quantum Computing, Math, and Physics (QCaMP): Introducing quantum computing in high schools. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16788

article_title: Quantum Computing, Math, and Physics (QCaMP): Introducing quantum computing in high schools
citation: Megan Ivory, Alisa Bettale, Rachel Boren, Ashlyn D. Burch, Jake Douglass, Lisa Hackett, Boris Kiefer, Alina Kononov, Maryanne Long, Mekena Metcalf, Tzula B. Propp, Mohan Sarovar. (2023). Quantum Computing, Math, and Physics (QCaMP): Introducing quantum computing in high schools. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16788
title: IBM Quantum Composer final project: group research exercise characterizing assigned quantum devices
description: The camp culminated in a hands-on research exercise using IBM's cloud-based quantum computers, reflecting the authors' guiding principle that "the best way to learn how a quantum computer works is to actually use one." Participants were introduced to the IBM Quantum Composer, a visual drag-and-drop interface requiring no prerequisite programming experience, then divided into small groups, each assigned one IBM quantum computer. Groups evaluated CNOT error and readout error to predict which computer would perform best, ran five experiments for each single- and multi-qubit circuit, recorded outcomes for statistical analysis, and compared measured error rates to other groups' results and IBM's specified errors. The authors report the main outcome was reinforcement of the scientific method through critical thinking and hands-on experimentation.
requirements: Access to IBM's publicly available cloud quantum computers and the Quantum Composer interface; prior camp instruction in gates, superposition, probability, and statistics
target_learners: High school students and teachers in small working groups
target_learning_goals: Characterizing quantum device error rates, interpreting measurement histograms, recognizing correlations in Bell-state measurement outcomes, and practicing the scientific method
examples: Groups ran five experiments per single- and multi-qubit circuit on their assigned IBM quantum computer, with the multi-qubit circuit designed to generate Bell states illustrating correlations in measurement outcomes
key_sources: Megan Ivory, Alisa Bettale, Rachel Boren, Ashlyn D. Burch, Jake Douglass, Lisa Hackett, Boris Kiefer, Alina Kononov, Maryanne Long, Mekena Metcalf, Tzula B. Propp, Mohan Sarovar. (2023). article_title: Quantum Computing, Math, and Physics (QCaMP): Introducing quantum computing in high schools
citation: Megan Ivory, Alisa Bettale, Rachel Boren, Ashlyn D. Burch, Jake Douglass, Lisa Hackett, Boris Kiefer, Alina Kononov, Maryanne Long, Mekena Metcalf, Tzula B. Propp, Mohan Sarovar. (2023). Quantum Computing, Math, and Physics (QCaMP): Introducing quantum computing in high schools. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16788
title: Link outreach lesson topics explicitly to existing science standards so teachers can integrate them into their classrooms
description: To aid teachers in incorporating QIST lesson modules in their classrooms, QCaMP linked each topic covered with relevant Next Generation Science Standards, QIS Key Concepts for K-12 Physics from the National Q-12 Education Partnership, and AP Physics 2 learning objectives. The focus was to expand on NGSS Disciplinary Core Idea PS4: Waves and Their Applications in Technologies for Information Transfer, so that "teachers can build upon classical physics already covered in their classrooms to transition into quantum concepts." Table II maps each camp topic to the corresponding QIS key concepts, NGSS standards, and AP Physics 2 objectives, making the alignment explicit for classroom transfer.
requirements: Camp topics must be mapped to the relevant standards documents (NGSS, Q-12 QIS Key Concepts, AP Physics 2 learning objectives) in a reference table teachers can consult
constraints: Some topics, such as entanglement and quantum logic and gates, have no reference in the NGSS or AP Physics 2 frameworks per Table II
target_learners: Middle and high school teachers seeking to integrate quantum topics into existing courses
target_learning_goals: Transitioning from classical wave physics standards to introductory quantum concepts in high school instruction
examples: Wave-particle duality was linked to NGSS HS-PS4-3 and specific AP Physics 2 topics, while quantum computing applications were linked to HS-PS4-2 and HS-ETS1-4

article_title: QCaMP: A 4-Week Summer Camp Introducing High School Students to Quantum Information Science and Technology
citation: Megan Ivory, Jan Balewski, Alisa Bettale, Jaden Brewer, Rachel Boren, Daan Camps, Lisa Hackett, Martin Juarez, Alina Kononov, Kan-Heng Lee, Maryanne Long, Andy Mounce, Susan Mniszewski, Ravi K. Naik, Scott Pakin, Ernesto Sanchez. (2025). QCaMP: A 4-Week Summer Camp Introducing High School Students to Quantum Information Science and Technology. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15977
title: QCaMP curriculum model: accessible QIST modules plus professional development and project-based learning
description: QCaMP is a 4-week summer camp in which national-laboratory QIST researchers collaboratively developed modules on quantum computing, sensing, and communication. Modules were "developed to be accessible to a broad range of students by avoiding any prerequisite math, physics, or computer science courses" and "incorporated experiential and active, hands-on learning wherever possible", with embedded quick multiple-choice and short-answer checks for understanding. The 4-week format added project-based learning, professional development, and lab tours alongside lessons.
requirements: Only prerequisite is Algebra 1; students must be 16 years old by the first day of camp
Quick multiple choice and short answer questions incorporated throughout modules to check understanding and allow instructors to revisit concepts
constraints: Modules avoid requiring prior advanced math, physics, chemistry, or programming classes
target_learners: High school students (grades 9–12 and college freshmen)
target_learning_goals: Awareness of and pathways into careers in quantum information science and technology
Foundational QIST concepts spanning quantum computing, sensing, and communication
examples: 2024 camp ran 7 hours/day, Monday–Friday, July 1–26, with cohorts in Berkeley CA, Albuquerque NM, and Santa Fe NM
key_sources: Megan Ivory, Jan Balewski, Alisa Bettale, Jaden Brewer, Rachel Boren, Daan Camps, Lisa Hackett, Martin Juarez, Alina Kononov, Kan-Heng Lee, Maryanne Long, Andy Mounce, Susan Mniszewski, Ravi K. article_title: QCaMP: A 4-Week Summer Camp Introducing High School Students to Quantum Information Science and Technology
citation: Megan Ivory, Jan Balewski, Alisa Bettale, Jaden Brewer, Rachel Boren, Daan Camps, Lisa Hackett, Martin Juarez, Alina Kononov, Kan-Heng Lee, Maryanne Long, Andy Mounce, Susan Mniszewski, Ravi K. Naik, Scott Pakin, Ernesto Sanchez. (2025). QCaMP: A 4-Week Summer Camp Introducing High School Students to Quantum Information Science and Technology. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15977
title: QCaMP student research projects in weeks 3–4
description: During the last two weeks, student groups completed largely student-driven projects with mentor guidance including daily check-ins, developing "skills in collaboration, experimental design, troubleshooting, and synthesizing their results to be communicated clearly through a scientific-style poster". Nine projects are listed in Table III: two QKD tabletop experiments (ThorLabs and University of Waterloo kits), double-slit interference (TeachSpin), quantum eraser, Planck's constant with LEDs, quantum sensing with a photoluminescence microscope, quantum simulation and quantum machine learning with VQE, quantum games, and quantum annealing on Star Battle puzzles.
requirements: Project equipment such as commercially available kits or instructor support (e.g., QICK-DAWG for quantum sensing)
constraints: D-Wave prohibits providing accounts on their cloud platform, Leap, to minors, so the quantum annealing project ran on a local classical simulated annealing simulator
The quantum annealing project required more Python training than the Python Primer provided
target_learning_goals: Experimental design, troubleshooting, collaboration, and science communication through scientific posters
examples: All students in the QKD project groups were able to explain the BB84 protocol in multiple ways by the end of the project
The quantum games group built a working prototype video game without any starter code

article_title: From Research to Resources: Assessing Student Understanding and Skills in Quantum Computing
citation: Thacker, B., Wang, J., Zhang, Y., Tran, Q. B., Vemula, D. S., & Kushimo, T. (2025). From Research to Resources: Assessing Student Understanding and Skills in Quantum Computing. NSF grant DUE 2235464. https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/?AwardId=2235464
title: Research-based mini-tutorials for an introductory quantum computing course
description: A set of ten short in-class tutorials patterned after research-based physics tutorials (e.g., University of Washington) but "shorter, designed to be done in 20-30 minutes, and focus on enhancing the ability to apply important concepts and skills covered in class." Topics include probability via Stern-Gerlach, half adder, single qubit gates, Bell states, entangled states, phase kickback, teleportation, Deutsch, Deutsch-Jozsa, and Quantum Fourier Transform. Each tutorial requires students to apply a concept in a different context or representation than first covered, e.g., answering the same question in matrix, Dirac, and Bloch sphere forms.
requirements: Not the student's first exposure to the concept or skill; students must apply it in a different context than initially covered in class
constraints: The authors identify needed revisions: the entanglement and phase kickback mini-tutorials should be modified, and modifications are needed for rotation gates and the quantitative part of the teleportation mini-tutorial
target_learners: upper-level undergraduate physics, computer engineering, electrical engineering, and interdisciplinary students in an introductory QC course
target_learning_goals: apply QC concepts and skills in theoretical analyses of quantum computing circuits and protocols
examples: In the Single Qubit Gates mini-tutorial students answered the same question in three representations (matrix, Dirac, Bloch sphere); in the teleportation mini-tutorial students first described teleportation qualitatively then worked through the circuit starting with a different Bell state than used in class.
key_sources: Thacker, B., Wang, J., Zhang, Y., Tran, Q. B., Vemula, D. S., & Kushimo, T. (2025). From Research to Resources: Assessing Student Understanding and Skills in Quantum Computing. NSF grant DUE 2235464. https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/?AwardId=2235464

article_title: Teaching quantum computing to computer science students: Review of a hands-on quantum circuit simulation practical
citation: Florian Krötz, Xiao-Ting Michelle To, Korbinian Staudacher, Dieter Kranzlmüller. (2025). Teaching quantum computing to computer science students: Review of a hands-on quantum circuit simulation practical. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17218
title: QCP: a deliberately simple text-file quantum circuit representation used to force gate-level thinking
description: QCP (Quantum Computing Practical) is the circuit representation used in the course: text files whose first line contains the number of qubits and each following line one gate in the format gateName[parameter][controlqubit(s)] targetqubit. It "dispenses with advanced features such as multiple quantum registers, classical registers, and conditional gates". The authors avoided Qiskit, Cirq, and OpenQASM because existing software abstracts away underlying quantum computing concepts; the representation is kept simple so writing a parser in another language is not difficult. Reference implementations are provided in Python and C.
requirements: A reference implementation in Python and C is provided to students; the simple format is intended to make writing a parser in another language feasible.
constraints: QCP omits registers, classical registers, and conditional gates, so it cannot express circuits relying on those features.
target_learners: graduate computer science students in the practical
target_learning_goals: thinking about quantum computing at the gate level
understanding how a quantum state is represented and modified by unitaries
examples: A two-qubit Bell-state circuit is written as a file with the line 2, then h 0, then cx 0 1.
key_sources: Florian Krötz, Xiao-Ting Michelle To, Korbinian Staudacher, Dieter Kranzlmüller. (2025). Teaching quantum computing to computer science students: Review of a hands-on quantum circuit simulation practical. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17218

article_title: Assessing student learning in quantum computing: Lessons from developing a test item on phase kickback
citation: Josephine C. Meyer, Steven J. Pollock, Bethany R. Wilcox, Gina Passante. (2026). Assessing student learning in quantum computing: Lessons from developing a test item on phase kickback. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22388
title: Quantum Computing Conceptual Survey (QCCS)
description: The QCCS is a closed-form, multiple-choice conceptual assessment of quantum computing comprising 20 items (including Item 15) mapped to 21 assessment objectives grouped into 5 overarching concepts. The authors "intend for QCCS to provide a reliable means for assessing student learning across diverse course contexts." Content coverage was constrained via a faculty survey, "selecting only topics assessed by at least 80% of theN= 68surveyed faculty," and the instrument underwent iterative validation using classical test theory and Rasch analysis plus student and instructor interviews.
requirements: Dichotomous scoring to support Rasch modeling; items must align with objectives, meet statistical benchmarks, perform well in interviews, and produce interpretable incorrect-answer patterns
constraints: The paper explicitly does not argue the instrument's validity and reliability in detail, referring readers to a companion validation paper
target_learners: students in introductory quantum information science courses across diverse US institutions
target_learning_goals: quantum computing fundamentals: mathematical foundations, entanglement, superposition and measurement, quantum gates, quantum circuit diagrams
examples: Item 15 was piloted in four versions across fall 2023 through fall 2025, accumulating 271, 621, 346, and 777 student responses respectively
key_sources: Josephine C. Meyer, Steven J. Pollock, Bethany R. Wilcox, Gina Passante. (2026). Assessing student learning in quantum computing: Lessons from developing a test item on phase kickback. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22388

article_title: Measuring student understanding in quantum computing: Development and validation of the Quantum Computing Conceptual Survey
citation: Josephine C. Meyer, Molly Griston, Gina Passante, Steven J. Pollock, and Bethany R. Wilcox (2026). Measuring student understanding in quantum computing: Development and validation of the Quantum Computing Conceptual Survey. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14459
title: Three-facet construct definition for quantum computing conceptual understanding: representations, properties, and evolution
description: The QCCS operationalizes its construct as 'the ability to reason about the representations, properties, and evolution of single- and multi-qubit systems.' The three facets are 'conceptually interdependent': representations supply the formal language, evolution describes how properties change, and many items require their intersection, such as reading a circuit diagram to judge whether a gate produces entanglement. The authors present this as a preliminary operationalization, not a complete theory of knowledge in the domain.
requirements: The construct definition 'relied on triangulation across several complementary sources of evidence': a systematic domain analysis of introductory QIS courses, instructor reports on important and difficult concepts, and existing research on student reasoning and difficulties.
constraints: The authors state they 'do not claim to have established a comprehensive construct map or learning progression for quantum computing'; the theoretical foundations for a detailed construct map remain underdeveloped.
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in introductory QIS courses
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of quantum computing fundamentals including qubits, superposition, entanglement, gates, measurement, and circuit diagrams
key_sources: Josephine C. Meyer, Molly Griston, Gina Passante, Steven J. Pollock, and Bethany R. Wilcox (2026). Measuring student understanding in quantum computing: Development and validation of the Quantum Computing Conceptual Survey. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14459

article_title: Maple's Quantum Chemistry Package in the Chemistry Classroom
citation: Jason M. Montgomery and David A. Mazziotti. (2020). Maple's Quantum Chemistry Package in the Chemistry Classroom. https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.10968
title: Guided computational lessons pairing visualization of abstract quantum concepts with model-chemistry exploration
description: The QCP lessons follow a reusable instructional pattern: students first visualize an abstract concept (e.g., molecular orbitals or particle-in-a-box wavefunctions) with simple commands, then explore 'more complex connections between a model chemistry (electronic structure method and underlying atomic orbital basis set) and the resulting energies and molecular properties.' Each lesson provides learning objectives, pre-written code, and a narrative that guides the student, and worksheets can be modified by students or instructors to fit class needs.
requirements: Access to Maple and the QCP; lessons are imported as a Workbook and executed
constraints: The article frames the activities as demonstrations of how the QCP might be exploited in the classroom; no classroom outcome data are reported
target_learners: undergraduate chemistry students from general chemistry to physical chemistry
target_learning_goals: connecting level of theory to molecular orbital properties
visualizing abstract quantum concepts
examples: In the HF lesson, students visualize the five occupied MOs and the LUMO using the DensityPlot3D command after geometry optimization
key_sources: Jason M. Montgomery and David A. Mazziotti. (2020). Maple's Quantum Chemistry Package in the Chemistry Classroom. https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.10968
